narrative:
The model predicted an 80% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class in both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that is strongly associated with bar exam difficulty.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 42, your score sits noticeably above the 37 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction somewhat toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Given the high predicted risk of failure, the school chose not to admit you. To improve your chances in the future, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program that addresses the specific gaps reflected in your lower class standing. Reapplying with clearer evidence of improvement could meaningfully change the outcome.
